title: Leonid Meteor Shower Peak Time Falls Before Leo Constellation Rises in US: Moonset Opens Best Window
excerpt: Leonid meteor shower viewers should skip the 6:45 p.m. ET Nov. 17 forecast peak, because Leo is still below the horizon across the US. The best Leonids viewing window opens near midnight, after the first-quarter Moon sets, and runs about 5 hours until dawn, at roughly 10 to 15 meteors per hour from
content:
The 2026 Leonid meteor shower's predicted maximum arrives at 6:45 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Nov. 17, more than four hours before the constellation Leo rises over New York (and even longer before it rises on the West Coast), so the best viewing window opens near midnight, when a first-quarter Moon sets and leaves roughly 5 hours of dark sky before dawn on Nov. 18. Skywatchers should expect at best 10 to 15 meteors an hour from a dark site, and no meteor storm is forecast.

The International Meteor Organization (IMO) lists the Leonids as active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30. Its calendar maximum, as relayed by Space.com and Star Walk, is 23:45 UT, which is 6:45 p.m. ET and 3:45 p.m. PT. Other predictions differ by hours: EarthSky expects the peak at 7 p.m. ET on Nov. 17 (0 UT on Nov. 18), and Star Walk reports forecaster Mikhail Maslov's alternative prediction of 11 a.m. ET (16:00 UT).

The IMO's own page labels the peak night Nov. 16-17 and says the Moon will be 45% full on it, and NASA also lists Nov. 16-17 as the peak night. That label and figure describe the night before the calendar's Nov. 17 maximum; a calculation with the PyEphem astronomy library puts the Moon at about 55% lit at 6:45 p.m. ET on Nov. 17.

Predicted Peak Lands While Leo Sits Below Horizon Across US

A shower's rate depends on how high its radiant stands above the horizon. The radiant is the point where meteors appear to originate, a perspective effect of parallel debris paths. At the IMO-calendar maximum, PyEphem calculations place Leo's radiant more than 27 degrees below the horizon in New York, 26 degrees below in Chicago and 24 degrees below in Los Angeles, where the Sun is still about 11 degrees above the horizon at 3:45 p.m. PT. Leo will clear the horizon near 10:57 p.m. ET in New York.

Showers also strengthen after midnight because the observer's side of Earth then turns toward the direction of Earth's orbit. That is why Farmers' Almanac gives roughly midnight to 5:30 a.m. local time as the prime window.

Midnight Moonset Opens Roughly 5 Hours of Moon-Free Sky

The Moon will reach first quarter at 6:48 a.m. ET on Nov. 17, and by the predicted maximum it will be technically waxing gibbous, just past first quarter. A first-quarter Moon sets near midnight on average, which is why Space.com says it sets before the best early-morning hours.

PyEphem calculations give moonset and astronomical dawn, the moment the Sun is 18 degrees below the horizon, for four cities; times are approximate to within a few minutes. Orbital Radar's independent New York forecast lists moonset at 11:55 p.m., within one minute of the PyEphem figure.

This year's Moon is not a crescent: the New Moon fell on Nov. 9, at 2:02 a.m. ET, so the Moon is a waxing, half-lit disk on peak night.

What Time Is Best to Watch Leonids Near You?

Plan to be outside from moonset until dawn, with counts building as Leo climbs. Orbital Radar's New York forecast singles out about 4:20 a.m. ET, when the radiant stands 59 degrees high, a figure PyEphem calculations reproduce. Space Informer suggests 2 a.m. until dawn. NASA advises looking away from Leo, because foreshortening makes meteors near the radiant look short.

Nights on either side of the peak are nearly as good, Orbital Radar says. In New York, the Moon will set at 10:52 p.m. ET on Nov. 16, giving about 6 hours 20 minutes of Moon-free sky, but not until 1:00 a.m. ET on Nov. 19 for the Nov. 18 evening, shrinking that window to about 4 hours 10 minutes.

Dark Sites Beat City Centers by Up to 10 Meteors Per Hour

Orbital Radar's New York forecast projects up to 11 meteors an hour from a dark site, 4 to 5 from a suburb and 1 to 2 from a city center. Skyglow explains the gap: densely populated areas can run about 100 times brighter than a natural dark sky, compared with about 40 times brighter for a full Moon.

Dust-Trail Models Time Leonid Storms Within Minutes; Next Large Outburst Forecast Is 2033

Leonid meteoroids come from comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the Sun about every 33 years. The comet travels a retrograde orbit inclined about 162.5 degrees to Earth's orbital plane, so its debris meets Earth nearly head-on at about 71 km/s (44 miles per second). The comet's nucleus measures about 3.6 km (2.2 miles) across.

Storms do not follow a 33-year clock. Each comet pass leaves a dust trail that planets and radiation forces shift over time, and Earth produces an outburst only when it crosses a young, dense trail. Astronomers David Asher and Robert McNaught timed the 1999 bursts to within about 10 minutes by modeling the stream from each comet passage, though they underestimated the peak intensity.

The Leonids produced storms in 1833, 1866, 1966 and again from 1999 to 2002, and NASA puts the last storm in 2002; astronomers define a storm as at least 1,000 meteors an hour. Star Walk reports one forecast for Nov. 17, 2033 reaches a ZHR of 300 to 400, while a newer model suggests up to 1,400, a rate Star Walk calls uncertain. The IMO's outlook says the best to hope for until 2030 is peaks of about 10 an hour, plus perhaps an occasional weak outburst, and notes that Earth meets no dense debris until 2099.

ZHR of 10 to 15 Marks Ceiling That Low Radiant and City Glow Cut Further

The zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) counts the meteors one observer would see per hour with the radiant overhead and stars down to magnitude 6.5 visible. The IMO lists a ZHR of 10, while Star Walk and Space.com say up to 15, and EarthSky quotes 10 to 15 meteors an hour under a dark sky without giving a ZHR. The commonly applied correction cuts the observed rate roughly in half when the radiant sits 30 degrees above the horizon, though that formula is disputed. NASA's fast-facts table goes lower, listing fewer than 3 meteors an hour under dark skies.

Alpha Monocerotids and November Orionids Follow Under Brighter Moon

Two minor showers follow: the Alpha Monocerotids peak Nov. 21-22, about two days before the Full Moon, and the November Orionids peak Nov. 27-28 at a ZHR of about 3, with moonlight limiting both to their brightest meteors. The Full Moon arrives at 9:53 a.m. ET on Nov. 24.

Best Plan Is Midnight to Dawn at Darkest Site Within Reach

For most U.S. observers, the forecast hour of 6:45 p.m. ET is irrelevant: Leo is below the horizon, and a half-lit Moon is still up. The usable show runs from roughly midnight until astronomical dawn near 5 a.m. local time on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at about 10 to 15 meteors an hour at best from a dark site and 1 or 2 from a city center, with the nights of Nov. 16 and Nov. 18 as backups if clouds arrive.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time is best to watch the Leonid meteor shower?

Plan on the hours between roughly midnight and 5 a.m. local time on Wednesday, Nov. 18, when the Moon is down and Leo is climbing; Farmers' Almanac's best window runs to 5:30 a.m. Counts rise toward dawn as the radiant climbs, reaching 59 degrees high at 4:20 a.m. in New York, but astronomical twilight ends the dark window near 5 a.m.

Why does the predicted peak time not match the best time to watch?

The predicted maximum marks when Earth is forecast to cross the densest part of the dust stream, and that moment can fall while Leo is below the horizon or the Sun is up. At the IMO-calendar time of 6:45 p.m. ET, Leo's radiant is below the horizon in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles, and ZHR figures assume a radiant overhead.

How many Leonid meteors will I see in 2026?

Expect at most about 10 to 15 an hour from a dark site, and as few as 1 or 2 an hour from a city center.

When is the next Leonid meteor storm?

No storm is forecast for 2026. Star Walk lists Nov. 17, 2033 as the next date with a forecast of 300 to 400 meteors an hour in one estimate, and the comet's next perihelion is May 20, 2031.
